eea_parameters.name: Social network layers (~5/15/50/150)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: The ancestral social world was structured as a series of hierarchically inclusive, nested relationship layers, each roughly three times the size of the one inside it: an innermost support clique of ~5 close confidants who provided emotional and physical support, a sympathy group of ~15 (people whose loss would be deeply felt, contacted at least monthly), an affinity/band layer of ~50 (the typical overnight foraging camp of casual-but-close associates), and an active personal network of ~150 (the clan/tribal layer, the outer ceiling of stable, individually-known relationships). Each layer carried a qualitatively different grade of intimacy, obligation, and contact frequency, with the heaviest investment concentrated in the inner ~5-15. The ~150 outer figure is an illustrative central tendency, not a constant: traditional tribal and clan groupings cluster in the low hundreds. Its original derivation from the primate neocortex-ratio regression is contested (Lindenfors, Wartel & Lind 2021), so the specific number is treated as approximate; what is load-bearing is the nested layering, not the precise ceiling. This was the full architecture within which status was monitored and alliances tracked: a personally-known reference group bounded at ~150, not an anonymous mass.

eea_value.outer_ceiling_note: low hundreds; ~150 is an approximate central tendency, not a constant; the neocortex-ratio derivation is contested (Lindenfors 2021)

eea_parameters.modern_default: The modern environment delivers a radically inverted network shape: nominal friend/follower counts in the hundreds or thousands that vastly exceed the ~150 cognitive ceiling, while the layers that actually carry support and intimacy stay capacity-bounded. Online networks reproduce the same ~5/15 inner structure when genuine ties are measured (support clique ~4, sympathy group ~14, statistically indistinguishable from offline values), and mean platform friend counts hover near ~150-180, but the bulk of nominal connections are inactive labels rather than relationships (only ~27.6% of online 'friends' are reported as genuine). Inner-layer bonds decay back toward mere acquaintance without the face-to-face contact the architecture was built to expect; mediated contact slows but does not substitute for it. The result is a wide, shallow periphery of weak or fictive ties layered on top of a core that the larger network does not, and cannot, enlarge.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The mismatch is not in the inner-layer capacities themselves (still ~5/15/50/150, not technologically expandable) but between the number of ties the modern environment presents (hundreds to thousands of nominal contacts) and the number the brain can actually monitor and invest in (~150, with real support concentrated in the inner ~5-15). People with unusually large networks do not gain more close friends; they accumulate weakly-defined acquaintances. Status monitoring (M5) and alliance/reputation tracking (M11), evolved for a ~150 personally-known reference group, are now flooded by reference groups orders of magnitude larger and largely composed of strangers, while the trust-bearing inner layers remain capped and are under-fed when face-to-face contact is displaced.
eea_parameters.confidence_note:
Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): contested. Layered personal networks scaling by about 3 hold up in modern network data, much of it from Dunbar's group, while the 150 derivation fails re-analysis (Lindenfors, Wartel and Lind 2021) and forager groups are fluid (Bird et al. 2019). Weight of evidence: the layering holds; the exact layer sizes and the 150 ceiling are disputed, so treat them as approximate.

eea_parameters.name: Daily incidental movement load
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Across a foraging day, adults covered substantial ground on foot as a structural side-effect of acquiring food, water, and firewood and of moving between patches and camp - roughly 9-15 km/day (Hadza men ~7-10 mi, women ~5 mi plus hours of digging), with movement woven through the whole waking day rather than concentrated into a bout. Activity was modest in intensity but near-continuous and embedded: light chores, child-carrying, frequent sit-to-stand transitions, and active resting postures (squatting, kneeling, ground-sitting) that sustain low-level lower-limb muscle activity. Hunter-gatherer PAL is only modestly above a Western desk worker's (~1.8-1.9 vs ~1.6), so the EEA baseline is not 'extreme exertion' but 'movement is the unavoidable medium of subsistence.'

rest_hours_per_day.note: comparable to industrialized adults; difference is posture not amount

eea_parameters.modern_default: Movement has been extracted from subsistence and re-inserted, if at all, as discretionary 'exercise': set-aside, planned, dose-prescribed (e.g. 150 min/week guidelines), and separated from the rest of a chair-bound, motor-transported, indoor day. Most waking hours are spent in continuous chair-sitting that holds the lower limbs near-inactive, and total daily distance on foot collapses far below the ancestral range.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The gap is not a calorie or PAL gap (these are surprisingly close) but a distributional one: ancestral movement was low-intensity, continuous, and obligatory; modern movement is optional, bunched, and easily skipped, leaving long uninterrupted muscular-inactivity bouts that the body never encountered. The mismatch is in HOW the day's muscle activity is spread, not in gross energy turnover.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Incidental all-day movement woven into the fabric of living (errands, carrying, standing, walking between activities, active rest postures) - NOT a set-aside 'exercise' session. The functional target is the continuous distribution of low-level activity across waking hours, not weekly minutes of vigorous training.
eea_parameters.confidence_note:
Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): tested many times. Forager activity of over 100 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous movement and activity levels modestly above Western ones are found across populations (Pontzer, Wood and Raichlen 2018); the kilometre band and rest figures are Hadza only.

Earlier grading notes (rubric v1, kept for the record): Grade DOWNGRADED from 'replicated' to 'theoretical' on adversarial review. Two reasons: (a) this is a mismatch interpretation (embedded/continuous vs modern bunched movement), which the grade rules require to stay theoretical; (b) the headline quantitative claim - the 9-15 km/day band and the PAL/MVPA/rest figures - is anchored to a narrow source base (Lieberman/work 57 supplies 196,197,198,195; the single Raichlen/Pontzer 2020 paper/work 63 supplies 288,289; one author/work 64 supplies 427), i.e. essentially Hadza-population data filtered through two source-works, not broad multi-study full-text convergence. What IS robust and converges across these full-text sources is the QUALITATIVE picture: movement is embedded not bout-shaped, active-rest posture matters, and forager PAL is only ~15% above a sedentary Westerner's. Cor must not hide the genuine tension: the same data show hunter-gatherers rest ~9.9h/day and are only modestly more active, so 'we evolved to move constantly and hard' is itself partly myth - the defensible claim is continuity-of-movement and active-rest posture, not heroic exertion. The specific km band is approximate and population-variable.

evidence.author_quote: Among the many studies of the Hadza, one asked forty-six Hadza adults to wear lightweight heart rate monitors for several days. According to these sensors, the average adult Hadza spends a grand total of three hours and forty minutes a day doing light activities and two hours and fourteen minutes a day doing moderate or vigorous activities. Although these few hours of hustling and bustling per day make them about twelve times more active than the average American or European, by no stretch of the imagination could one characterize their workloads as backbreaking. On average, the women walk five miles a day and dig for several hours, whereas the men walk between seven and ten miles a day. And when they aren't being very active, they typically rest or do light work.

eea_parameters.name: Daily subsistence work-hours (contested)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: QUALITATIVE ONLY. The duration of daily subsistence effort in the EEA is genuinely unresolved and must not be stated as a number. The 'original affluent society' position (Sahlins/Lee) reads the data as short food-quest hours and ample leisure; the opposing reading (Kaplan/Hawkes/Pontzer, and Lieberman's own qualifications) emphasizes that total productive effort includes processing, childcare, toolwork, and travel, and that activity is modest-intensity but spread across the day. What the full-text evidence DOES support qualitatively is that forager workloads are not 'backbreaking' and that overall energetic activity is only modestly above a sedentary Westerner's - but this does not license any specific daily work-hour figure.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Modern work is organized around fixed, externally scheduled, often long and boundary-less hours (clock-time labor, always-on digital availability) - a structurally different time-architecture from intermittent, self-paced, weather- and resource-contingent subsistence effort, regardless of what the ancestral hour-count actually was.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The defensible mismatch is in the STRUCTURE of work-time (externally clocked, continuous, boundary-less vs. intermittent, self-paced, contingent), not in any claimed reduction or increase in daily hours. Asserting a specific ancestral work-hour number - in either direction - would import a contested anthropological position as if it were settled, which it is not.
eea_parameters.resolution_unit: Self-paced, resource-contingent, intermittently-bounded work time - the time ARCHITECTURE (when and how effort is scheduled and bounded), not a target number of daily hours.
eea_parameters.confidence_note:
Grade, rubric v2 (6 Nov 2026): contested. Weight of evidence: once processing, travel and childcare are counted, forager work time is longer than the short-hours figures, while foragers still have more leisure than neighbouring farmers (Dyble et al. 2019); no single daily hour figure is supported.

evidence.author_quote: When Herman Pontzer and his colleagues measured daily energy expenditures in the Hadza, they were surprised to find that the highly active Hadza spend about the same total number of calories per day as sedentary industrialized people with the same lean body weight. In addition, when Pontzer and colleagues collected energetic data from adults in many countries including the United States, Ghana, Jamaica, and South Africa, they observed that more active people spent only slightly more calories per day than more sedentary people who weighed the same. In addition, individuals who were more physically active didn't have total energy budgets as high as their exertions would predict. How could someone who spent five hundred extra calories a day exercising not have a total energy budget that is five hundred calories higher? The proposed explanation is that people's total energy budgets are constrained: if I use five hundred extra calories walking, I'll spend less energy on my resting metabolism to help pay for my exertions.

eea_parameters.name: Status reference group (ranked against people who know you)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: A forager's standing was judged by people who knew them. Daily life ran in a camp of about 30 (Hadza) inside a lifetime pool of roughly 1,000 people known by name (Ache, Hadza). The status monitor weighs this local audience most: across 15 small-scale communities (899 people), the shame people expected to feel over an act tracked how much their own community would think less of them (mean r 0.84) more closely than how other communities would (0.69). In four US studies, respect in one's face-to-face groups went with well-being more strongly than income or education did, and well-being rose and fell with that standing.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Rank can be compared against people who will never know you: celebrities, strangers' edited lives, follower and like counts. No study in Cor measures how many people a person compares themselves with online. The measured link between social media use and low mood is small (r about 0.1 in meta-analyses of adolescents) and near zero in time-use diaries.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The audience that sets a person's standing grows from a group that knows them to an open-ended field of strangers whose judgement the person cannot meet or change. The measured harm of online comparison is small, so the row predicts a shift in who the monitor compares against, and the size of the cost is open.

The local-ladder paper (Anderson et al. 2012) is US students and adults from one research group. Leary 1995 (ext 621) reads the sociometer as tuned to a small set of significant others; that reading is theoretical, the studies did not compare known people with strangers. Contested on the modern side: social media effect sizes are small (ext 103, 104) and near zero in time-use diaries (ext 102).

eea_parameters.name: How standing is earned (prestige and dominance)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Two routes to rank exist: dominance, through fear, and prestige, through skill that others choose to defer to. In experiments with strangers both routes work. In small-scale societies prestige is the stronger route to leadership (Chabu, Tsimane), and in mobile foragers a leader's influence is informal, tied to the situation, and rests on others choosing to follow. Authority from skill stays inside the activity: Mbendjele BaYaka specialists are consulted on elephant hunting, healing or ritual and can oblige no one, and Tsimane fishing-trip organisers rotate across households and take no extra fish. Respect is different: where it was measured (one Tsimane village of 57 men, the Chabu), fighting ability, influence and respect sat with the same few men.

eea_value.tsimane_task_leaders: only 7 of 31 regular households never organised a fishing trip (von Rueden et al. 2014)

eea_parameters.modern_default: Standing is earned in large organisations and markets among people who mostly do not know each other, through titles, pay and audience size. Formal authority carries across domains: a manager commands in every part of the job, and wealth or fame buys influence outside the skill that earned it.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: In the forager record, command stayed inside the activity and could be refused; modern rank carries command across domains and is hard to refuse or leave. The concentration of respect in a few people is the part that may be old: two forager-horticulturalist samples show it.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): contested. The two-routes finding is tested many times (Cheng et al. 2013, ext 622; von Rueden et al. 2011, ext 623; Garfield and Hagen 2020, ext 624). The 'authority stays inside the activity' clause holds for command in Mbendjele BaYaka ethnography (Lewis 2014) and Tsimane task leadership (von Rueden et al. 2014) and fails for respect in a Tsimane village (von Rueden et al. 2008) and among the Chabu (ext 624). Lean: holds for command, fails for respect. Both quantitative counter-samples are semi-sedentary, which leaves room for mobile bands to differ. The modern side is described, not measured here. Background-tier evidence cited (abstract or book only): ext 689, 732.

eea_parameters.name: What standing buys (children)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Across 33 non-industrial societies, higher-status men had more children (meta-analysis of 288 results, overall r 0.19). The effect in foragers (Zr 0.18) was about the same as in farmers and herders. Status worked mostly through more mates and more births, less through fewer child deaths, and the effect on surviving children was about a third smaller where marriage was monogamous. eea_parameters.name: Wealth gaps (low to moderate in foragers)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Forager material inequality was low to moderate. Weighted wealth Gini coefficients were 0.25 for hunter-gatherers and 0.27 for horticulturalists, against 0.42 for pastoralists and 0.48 for farmers, where land and livestock can be owned and inherited (21 small-scale populations). Across eleven kinds of forager wealth most Ginis fell between 0.2 and 0.5; the two material measures averaged 0.36. House sizes at 63 archaeological sites give the same order: median Gini 0.17 at hunter-gatherer sites, 0.35 at agricultural sites.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Wealth Gini coefficients in modern states are far higher: about 0.80 for the USA in 2000 and 0.73 for China, figures Kohler et al. cite from other studies. Among the Ju/'hoansi, 44 years of cash income produced large material differences even between neighbours.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: Wealth gaps went from small, mostly in body and skill, to very large, mostly in owned and inherited property, and the distance between top and bottom is now visible to everyone. eea_parameters.name: Famous strangers (one-way bonds)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Everyone a forager knew of could be met. The lifetime pool of individually known people was about 1,000, and the people one heard about in stories were part of the same regional network, tied to people one knew. A person you saw and heard often knew you back.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Media supply one-way bonds with people who do not know you exist. In a quota sample of 2,028 Hungarian adults, 39% had a favourite celebrity, and on the authors' scale 4.5% of adults and 8.5% of 18 to 34 year olds had a high level of admiration. Of 151 US early adolescents, 61% thought of their favourite media figure as a relationship partner: girls mostly as a friend, boys more often as a mentor.

eea_parameters.name: Size of "us" (the language group)

eea_parameters.name: Contact between groups (visiting and exchange alongside hostility)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Forager bands were linked. Among the Hadza and Ache, adults who were in-laws or ritual partners interacted across bands more often, and in-law ties mattered about as much as blood ties. In 1974 each Ju/'hoansi adult kept about 15 gift-exchange partners living 2 to 200 km away and spent on average 4.4 months a year living with them. Humans form peaceful ties between groups, which chimpanzees do not. Hostility was also part of the record: the Ache and Hadza had hostile relations with neighbouring ethnic groups and no long-distance trade, and in 20 of 21 mobile forager societies about 15% of recorded killings were between groups.
eea_parameters.modern_default: Contact between large groups runs through trade, media and institutions; most members of two groups never meet, marry or visit each other.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: Forager groups were tied by marriage, visits and gifts that ran through people one knew, alongside real hostility toward some neighbours. Modern intergroup ties rarely run through personal relationships.
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested once per population. Contact between bands within one language group is documented in several populations (Hill et al. 2014; Wiessner and Huang 2022, ext 752). Cor has no measured rate of marriage or trade between different language groups. Hill et al. 2014 warn that their two populations understate contact because both had hostile neighbours. eea_parameters.name: Killing between groups (frequency contested)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Lethal raids between groups occurred among foragers, and in some populations they were frequent. How often they happened among mobile Pleistocene foragers is not settled. Bowles compiled 23 sources and found war deaths averaged 14% of all deaths (archaeological 12%, ethnographic 16%; single sites 0% to 46%), in samples that include sedentary and contact-period groups. Fry and Soderberg found that in 21 mobile forager band societies most of 148 recorded killings had one killer and one victim; about a third were between groups, but 38 of those 50 came from one society, the Tiwi, and in the other 20 societies about 15% were. A phylogenetic estimate puts all killing by other humans at about 2% of deaths.

eea_parameters.name: What marks someone as "them" (alliance cues)
eea_parameters.eea_baseline: Foragers marked groups by language, dialect, ritual and marriage ties, and rarely met people genetically distant enough to look like another race. The tested part: the mind sorts people by alliance, and the sorting can be redrawn within minutes. When team membership cut across race, US participants sorted people by race less (a preregistered replication with 463 people found the drop at a smaller size; race was not erased). Arbitrary labels produce favouritism toward one's own group; a meta-analysis of cooperation experiments gives d 0.32, larger when outcomes depend on each other, and driven more by favouring 'us' than by harming 'them'.

eea_value.ingroup_favouritism_d: 0.32 overall; 0.19 bare labels; 0.42 interdependent (Balliet et al. 2014)

eea_parameters.modern_default: Large labelled groups (parties, nations, teams) supply alliance cues without any shared life. In the US, the gap between feelings toward one's own and the other party grew from 22.64 to 40.87 points on a 0 to 100 scale between 1978 and 2016, driven by colder feelings toward the other side. The rise is not general: across 12 OECD democracies six saw it fall. Posts about the political out-group are shared more (each out-group word about 67% higher odds, US media and Congress). Sports fans claim a team's win as their own and say 'we' twice as often after a win.
eea_parameters.gap_statement: The alliance-sorting system now runs on labels for groups of millions, with no shared life and no repeated contact, and media reward posts about 'them'. That moralised posts spread more is contested (Brady et al. 2017 against Burton et al. 2021).
eea_parameters.confidence_note: Grade, rubric v2 (11 Nov 2026): tested many times for 'us and them are drawn from alliance cues and can be redrawn' (Kurzban et al. 2001; Voorspoels et al. 2014 preregistered replication; Pietraszewski et al. 2014; Balliet et al. 2014 meta-analysis). mechanism_ages.part: defensive output centre (periaqueductal gray)
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least 460 million years, likely about 460 to 535
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic circuit in the first vertebrates: a periaqueductal gray homologue, the command centre for freezing, flight and defensive fighting, shared with lampreys

Older figures in the A sources (haitina2007: 525 fossil, 564 molecular; Grillner lab: about 500, or over 560) are cited round numbers and are superseded by T. Defensive behaviour itself is older (invertebrates have it) but uses non-homologous circuits (ledoux2012), so it does not date the human system.

mechanism_ages.note: Date from group T: crown tetrapods 337 to 351 (Wardie Shales minimum; molecular 338 to 354). Possibly older: a fish pallial region may be the amygdala homologue (portavella2004, moreno2007), which would push it to the bony-fish ancestor, group T crown osteichthyans 420.7 to 444.9 (portavella2004 says some 400 million years); that extension rests on one lab's goldfish lesions and is graded thin, so it is kept out of the label. No amygdala homologue has been identified in lamprey (suryanarayana2022), so the old field's all-vertebrates reading does not hold for this part.

mechanism_ages.age_label: at least 460 million years, likely about 460 to 535
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic circuit in the first vertebrates: striatum, pallidum and dopamine input with a habenula outcome-evaluation loop, shared with lampreys
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Frost-Nylen et al. 2024 and Suryanarayana et al. 2022 review lamprey tracing and physiology from essentially one lab; Yamamoto and Vernier 2011 doubt that lamprey and teleost diencephalic dopamine cells match the mammalian SNc/VTA. Weight leans toward homology on the later lamprey connectivity data.
mechanism_ages.note: Dates from group T crown vertebrates (fossil minimum 457.5, molecular 459.3 to 533.8); frostnylen2024 says about 500 million years, a cited round number. Yamamoto and Vernier place the conserved dopamine motor role at tetrapods (group T 337 to 351), which is the low end if the lamprey homology fails. This dates the general action-selection machinery that seeking runs on; it does not show reward seeking in lamprey.

mechanism_ages.part: mesolimbic reward pathway (midbrain dopamine to ventral striatum)
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 165 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the human form's reward-specific pathway, shown in all mammals studied, with a probable counterpart in birds, reptiles and frogs
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Yamamoto and Vernier 2011: anatomical resemblance of SNc/VTA and a proposed accumbens in birds, reptiles and amphibians; the authors call mesolimbic conservation less clear, and no non-mammal reward test is in these sources.
mechanism_ages.note: Lower bound is crown mammals (Panksepp: SEEKING in all mammals), group T 164.9 to 201.5. If the bird, reptile and frog anatomy holds up as homology it would be crown tetrapods (337 to 351), which is why the row is open-ended. The tetrapod reading is probable, not shown. Lamprey striatum has no clear ventral division (suryanarayana2022). The deep circuit row above is the better public figure for the seeking system's machinery; this row records that its reward-specific wiring is less certainly that old.

mechanism_ages.part: attachment and separation distress
mechanism_ages.age_label: about 165 to 200 million years (as old as the living mammals)
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic circuit in the first mammals: infant attachment and separation distress tied to a nursing mother, shared by the mammals tested
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest source: Panksepp's brain stimulation work showing the separation-distress system in every mammal tested; main weakness: one programme, species not itemised, no monotreme or marsupial data, and the link to lactation is inference.
mechanism_ages.note: Clade: crown Mammalia. Panksepp E267 says at least 150 million years; Oftedal puts milk-dependent young in mammal ancestors by about 210 million years ago, so the system may be older than crown mammals. Separation calls also occur in chicks, so the behaviour alone is not mammal-only. The field value ~200Myr (mammalian) sits at the top of the crown mammal range. Group T: crown mammals 164.9 to 201.5 (fossil), 164.8 to 204.7 (molecular).

mechanism_ages.part: oxytocin and vasotocin peptides
mechanism_ages.age_label: oxytocin gene about 420 to 470 million years (as old as the jawed vertebrates); its vasotocin parent is older
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the molecular toolkit, not the bonding system: vasotocin (vasopressin) is shared with invertebrate chordate relatives; oxytocin split off from it in the first jawed vertebrates
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest source: Theofanopoulou et al. 2021, synteny and phylogeny across 35 vertebrate genomes; main weakness: one group's reconstruction and only four invertebrate genomes.
mechanism_ages.note: Clade: crown Gnathostomata for oxytocin. These peptides were co-opted into mammalian attachment and maternal care; their age must not be printed as the age of attachment. Group T: crown gnathostomes 420.7 to 468.4. The min and max are for oxytocin only.

mechanism_ages.part: social play (rough-and-tumble)
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 60 million years (all primates play), possibly up to about 160 to 170 million years if marsupial and placental play are one system
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the human line's play system, which every living primate shares; play outside mammals evolved separately and is not part of this age
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest source: Burghardt 2014 (all primates play in all three ways) with Iwaniuk et al. 2001 (play across 15 mammal orders); main weakness: homology is inferred from distribution only, and Burghardt et al. 2024 list a shared mammal-wide play-fighting mechanism as an open question.
mechanism_ages.note: Lower bound: crown Primates. Upper bound if marsupial and placental play prove to be one inherited system: crown Theria. Rat play fighting (Pellis E218, E223) is the best-mapped circuit; the rodent and primate common ancestor (Euarchontoglires) is a possible intermediate bound, untested. The field text "absent in reptiles" is wrong: play is documented in turtles, lizards, crocodilians, fish and invertebrates (Burghardt 2014, Dinets 2015), but as independent origins. Group T: crown primates 56 to 66 (fossil), 67.3 to 69.1 (molecular); crown therians 156.3 to 169.6 (fossil). The max is the untested upper bound, not an estimate.

mechanism_ages.part: rank detection and rank-driven brain change (social behaviour network)
mechanism_ages.age_label: about 420 to 445 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic circuit in the first bony vertebrates: the social behaviour network that reads rank is homologous in fish, reptiles, birds and mammals
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Fernald and Maruska 2012, cichlid fish rank switching with network-wide gene activation, citing homology of the network in fish, reptiles and birds. Weakness: one lab's fish work and one review's summary of the homology; the primary comparative papers were not read.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: group T crown osteichthyans, 420.7 to 444.9 (Guiyu minimum; molecular composite 420.6 to 444.2). Clade: crown bony vertebrates (Osteichthyes: ray-finned fish plus tetrapods). Cartilaginous fish and lampreys were not covered by the source, so the circuit could be older. Serotonin-linked dominance in crayfish (Huber 1997) shows status behaviour in invertebrates, but no source claims it is the same inherited system, so it does not set the age.

mechanism_ages.part: rank-linked stress physiology, health and survival
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 25 to 34 million years in the human line; also seen in other mammal orders
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the human form in the primate line: rank-linked survival and stress physiology shared with baboons and macaques
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Snyder-Mackler et al. 2020, a multi-group review of long-term field studies showing status predicts survival in at least 12 species including baboons and macaques. Weakness: the species acquired social living separately several times, so the shared pattern is partly convergent and its inheritance within primates is inferred.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: group T crown catarrhines, 24.44 to 34.0. Clade for the human line: crown catarrhines (humans, apes, baboons, macaques). The pattern also appears in rabbits, meerkats, hyenas and ungulates, through several separate transitions to social living, so a single mammal-wide age would overstate homology. Sapolsky 2004 and 2005 (Cor works 91, 92) cover primate rank and health but were not reread here.

mechanism_ages.part: passivity default under prolonged uncontrollable stress (dorsal raphe serotonin)
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 60 to 90 million years; about 165 to 200 million years if all mammals share it, as the authors say
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic circuit as tested: shown in rats, mice and dogs and described by the authors as the default mammalian reaction
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Maier and Seligman 2016, rat dorsal raphe experiments showing passivity is the default and control is learned. Weakness: one group's rat work; "mammalian" is a generalisation, and older origins (a serotonin-linked stress state in flies) are untested for homology.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: the tested species (rats, mice, dogs) share an ancestor inside crown placentals; group T has no node for that ancestor (Boreoeutheria), so the floor uses the crown placental fossil minimum 61.6 and molecular 87.9 to 90.4 (contested between fossil and molecular readings). The authors' "mammalian" would mean crown mammals, 164.9 to 201.5. contested is set true for the dating, not the default itself. Minimum clade: the common ancestor of rodents and dogs (Boreoeutheria) as the tested species; the authors say mammalian, which would mean crown mammals. Serotonin is very old and flies show a stress-induced, serotonin-modulated inactivity state (Ries 2017), so the default may be much older, but no source tests homology.

mechanism_ages.part: prefrontal controllability detector (prelimbic, ventromedial prefrontal cortex)
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 60 to 90 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic circuit in the common ancestor of rodents and primates: the medial (agranular) prefrontal cortex that detects control in rats is homologous to the primate anterior cingulate region
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Maier and Seligman 2016 for the rat prelimbic detector, plus Laubach et al. 2018 for rodent to primate medial frontal homology. Weakness: the detector is one group's rat result, human evidence is a few imaging studies, and area-by-area homology is debated.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: the rodent and primate ancestor (Euarchontoglires) lies inside crown placentals and is not a group T node; floor from the crown placental fossil minimum 61.6, upper from the crown placental molecular range 87.9 to 90.4 (fossil and molecular readings disagree, hence contested). Clade: Euarchontoglires (rodents plus primates). No source read covers medial prefrontal cortex in other mammals, so it may be older. The granular lateral prefrontal cortex is primate-specific and is not the detector.

mechanism_ages.part: the human clock-gene system (CLOCK and BMAL1 with PERIOD and CRYPTOCHROME)
mechanism_ages.age_label: more than 500 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic clock-gene loop in the common ancestor of insects and vertebrates (bilaterian animals); its CLOCK, CYCLE/BMAL1 and cryptochrome parts reach back to the ancestor shared with sea anemones
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Rosbash 2009 summarises clock-gene orthology between flies and mammals found by many groups; the 500 million year figure is a cited lower bound for the insect-mammal split.
mechanism_ages.note: Label keeps Rosbash's sourced lower bound. Group T crown bilaterians: fossil 550.25 to 636.1 (minimum rests on Kimberella, disputed), molecular 595.7 to 688.3; if the main session prefers T, about 550 to 690 million years, contested at the minimum. Extension to the cnidarian-bilaterian ancestor (no group T node; it lies between crown animals, 550 to 833, and crown bilaterians) rests on one lab's sea anemone study and lacks Period, so it is kept out of the label (thin). The SCN as master clock is a vertebrate/mammalian arrangement and is not dated here (see unsourced).

mechanism_ages.part: daily clocks as a kind of system (cyanobacteria)
mechanism_ages.age_label: about 1 to 3.5 billion years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the oldest known daily clocks, in cyanobacteria; a separate invention that is not the ancestor of the human clock
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Dvornyk et al. 2003: one molecular-clock study; the full three-gene clock dates to about 1,000 million years, older parts (kaiB, kaiC) to 2,320 to 3,800 million years, with few kaiA sequences and two calibration points.
mechanism_ages.note: The old field (about 3 billion years, cyanobacteria onward) implied the human clock descends from the cyanobacterial one. It does not: the clock proteins are unrelated and the two systems arose separately (rosbash2009). Even the cyanobacterial three-gene clock is dated to about 1 billion years; 3.5 billion is the age of kaiB/kaiC parts, which alone are not shown to keep daily time. Keep this row off the human-system headline.

mechanism_ages.part: innate immunity and inflammatory signalling (pattern-recognition receptors such as Toll-like receptors)
mechanism_ages.age_label: about 550 to 830 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic system in the first animals: pattern-recognition receptors are found throughout the animal kingdom
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Flajnik and Kasahara 2010, a review of comparative immune genomics. Weakness: the animal-wide claim is one sentence citing others, and the date of the animal common ancestor rests on molecular clocks with a wide range.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: group T crown animals, fossil 550.25 to 833 (contested at the minimum, which rests on reading Kimberella as a bilaterian) and molecular 649.8 to 833.5. Clade: crown animals (Metazoa). "All multicellular" is wrong as homology: plants have their own expanded receptor families, and plants and fungi became multicellular separately. Brennan and Gilmore 2018 (Mol Biol Evol, Toll-like receptor origins) could tighten this but its OA copy sits behind a bot check and was not read.

mechanism_ages.part: adaptive immunity (RAG-based antibodies, T cell receptors, MHC)
mechanism_ages.age_label: about 420 to 470 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic system in the first jawed vertebrates (shared with sharks and rays)
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Flajnik and Kasahara 2010, summarising RAG, antibody, T cell receptor and MHC genes found in every jawed vertebrate class and absent in jawless fish. Weakness: the source gives only a round 500 million years; the fossil-calibrated date must come from group T.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: group T crown gnathostomes, 420.7 to 468.4 (Guiyu minimum; molecular composite 432.1 to 468.1). The source's round "500 million years" is a little older than this range; the fossil-calibrated range is used. Clade: crown jawed vertebrates (Gnathostomata); the source says the system has been "remarkably uniform over 500 million years"; take the fossil-calibrated range from group T. Lampreys and hagfish evolved a separate adaptive system (VLRs), so it is convergent and does not extend the human system's age; B-like and T-like lymphocyte lineages may predate the jawed and jawless split. Grade replicated holds only if that date is fossil-calibrated.

mechanism_ages.part: maternal care circuitry
mechanism_ages.age_label: about 165 to 200 million years (as old as the living mammals)
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic circuit in the first mammals: maternal care built around nursing (medial preoptic area, oxytocin, prolactin, dopamine), found in all living mammals
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest source: Rilling and Young 2014, a review of rodent circuit work with human parallels; main weakness: the circuit is shown in rodents and humans only, and its presence in all mammals is inferred from lactation (Oftedal 2012, abstract).
mechanism_ages.note: Clade: crown Mammalia. Oftedal dates milk-dependent young to about 210 million years ago in mammal ancestors (inference). The preoptic area also controls parental care in other vertebrates, so parts of the circuit may be older; not sourced here. Group T: crown mammals 164.9 to 201.5 (fossil).

mechanism_ages.part: human cooperative breeding (alloparenting)
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 2 million years (theory)
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the human form: routine care and provisioning of young by helpers other than the mother, unique among apes and evolved separately from cooperatively breeding monkeys
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest source: Burkart et al. 2014, one standardised test across 15 primate species, plus Burkart et al. 2025 placing the setting in early Homo about 2 million years ago; main weakness: the onset is inferred from life-history models and fossil ecology, never observed.
mechanism_ages.note: Burkart et al. 2025 argue cooperative breeding came before large brains and that weaning age fell already in australopithecines, so the true onset may be older than 2 million years. Competing scenarios (altriciality first, diet first) would put it later. Hrdy 2009 (Cor work 10) and Kramer 2010 (Cor work 193) are the standard sources but no extraction was read here. The max of 10 is only the bound set by the human-chimpanzee split (group T: 6.5 to 10, contested), not an estimate of onset.

mechanism_ages.part: the human form: a body that depends on high daily aerobic activity
mechanism_ages.age_label: about 2 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the human form: the shift to hunting and gathering, which made high daily aerobic activity normal and, on this argument, made health upkeep depend on it
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Raichlen and Alexander 2017 model paper: the two million year activity shift comes from cited fossil and archaeological work; the link to today's dependence on exercise is argued, not tested. Raichlen et al. 2012 (humans, dogs, ferrets) supports a running-linked reward but is one small study.
mechanism_ages.note: The source says around two million years. Group T has no genus Homo node; its notes carry the same about 2 million year genus figure from Eaton and Konner 1985 (E38, verified only from the preview paragraph). The old field (about 500 million years) has no source behind it: nothing found dates movement as a zeitgeber, anti-inflammatory or mood regulator across vertebrates (see unsourced).

mechanism_ages.part: reciprocal exchange and alliances in primates
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 25 to 34 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic behaviour in the common ancestor of humans, apes and Old World monkeys: reciprocal exchange seen in chimpanzees, baboons and macaques
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Schino and Aureli 2008, a meta-analysis of grooming reciprocation in 48 groups of 22 primate species. Weakness: behavioural correlation only; homology is inferred from distribution, and similar exchanges in coatis show the trait can arise separately.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: group T crown catarrhines, 24.44 to 34.0. Clade: crown catarrhines (Cosmides and Tooby name macaques and baboons; Schino and Aureli sample is dominated by macaques). Schino and Aureli call the pattern widespread across the primate order, which could push it older, but the species list was not read. Cosmides and Tooby give "at least" the human and chimpanzee ancestor, 5 to 10 million years in 1992 estimates, as a floor, and point further back to macaques and baboons.

mechanism_ages.part: third-party norm enforcement and large-scale reciprocity (human form)
mechanism_ages.age_label: younger than the human and chimpanzee split, about 7 to 10 million years ago; exact age unknown
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the human form: punishing violators on behalf of others, absent in chimpanzees in the one experiment that tested it
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Riedl et al. 2012, an experiment finding no third-party punishment in chimpanzees. Weakness: one study in one species read as abstract only; no source dates when in the human line this arose.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: upper bound from group T human vs chimpanzee, fossil 6.5 to 10 (contested), molecular 7 to 13. Upper bound: the human and chimpanzee common ancestor. No lower bound sourced; Tomasello et al. 2012 (Curr Anthropol, interdependence hypothesis) proposes Homo-era steps but its OA copies sit behind a bot check and were not read. Boehm (Cor works 9, 177) and Tomasello (work 14) are in Cor but were not reread.

mechanism_ages.part: pathogen and parasite avoidance behaviour (as a kind of behaviour)
mechanism_ages.age_label: found across the animal kingdom; no single age, since no source shows it is one inherited system
mechanism_ages.dates_what: a kind of behaviour found from nematodes and insects to fish, birds and mammals; no source shows it is one inherited system
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: Sarabian, Curtis and McMullan 2018, a cross-species overview with experiments in nematodes, bees and bonobos. Weakness: it documents breadth, not homology, and expects commonalities because every organism faces parasites.
mechanism_ages.note: The presence of the behaviour across animals is well documented; any single date for it would treat convergent solutions as one inherited system. No source traces a shared avoidance circuit between nematodes, insects and vertebrates.

mechanism_ages.part: contamination avoidance in primates (precursor of human pathogen disgust)
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 25 to 34 million years, if the primate response is the same system
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic response in the common ancestor of humans, apes and Old World monkeys: avoidance of faeces-contaminated food in bonobos, chimpanzees, macaques and mandrills
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest: bonobo and macaque contamination experiments summarised in Sarabian et al. 2018. Weakness: mostly one research group and few species; continuity with human disgust is argued, not tested.
mechanism_ages.note: Date: group T crown catarrhines, 24.44 to 34.0. Clade: crown catarrhines. The human disgust expression, its sexual domain and its moral extension have no dated source here: Curtis et al. 2011 show disgust is universal in humans, which makes it old within our species but does not date it. Moral disgust is human-only by definition and its age is unsourced.

mechanism_ages.part: brain appetite brake (leptin and melanocortin MC4 signalling that cut food intake)
mechanism_ages.age_label: more than 420 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic circuit in the first jawed vertebrates: leptin and brain melanocortin receptors that reduce food intake, shown in bony fish and mammals but not in lamprey brains
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Deck et al. 2017 review: injected leptin cut food intake in five fish species across several groups, as in mammals; fish leptin sequences differ a lot from mammalian leptin, and the lamprey evidence (Haitina et al. 2007) is one lab's.
mechanism_ages.note: Group T: crown osteichthyans 420.7 to 444.9 (the minimum, from the fish feeding experiments) and crown gnathostomes 420.7 to 468.4 (likely origin on Haitina's reading, since sharks express brain melanocortin receptors). It should be younger than crown vertebrates (460 to 535), since lamprey melanocortin receptors are not in the brain. Leptin as a fat-store signal is not shown in fish (deck2017 ext 1) and was not dated; the old field's 500 million years is too old for the brain appetite brake.

mechanism_ages.part: the human form: a larger daily energy budget and more body fat than other apes
mechanism_ages.age_label: less than about 6.5 to 10 million years
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the human form: faster metabolism and greater fat stores that evolved in the human line after it split from chimpanzees and bonobos
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Pontzer et al. 2016 (doubly labelled water, 141 humans, 56 apes): one study, zoo and sanctuary apes, small ape samples.
mechanism_ages.note: Pontzer shows the change happened in the human line but does not date it within that line; the upper limit is the human-chimpanzee split, group T fossil 6.5 to 10 (contested; molecular 7 to 13). Pontzer's constrained-energy finding (Cor work 61) is a within-lifetime adjustment measured in living adults and supports no age.

mechanism_ages.part: sexual desire: hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least 460 million years, likely about 460 to 535 (as old as the vertebrates)
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic hormonal circuit in the first vertebrates: GnRH from the hypothalamus driving the pituitary and gonads, already present in lampreys
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest source: Sower et al. 2012, lamprey GnRH peptides and receptors from a long lab programme; main weakness: one group's review, and its 550 million year lineage figure is not a calibrated node date.
mechanism_ages.note: Clade: crown Vertebrata (lamprey plus jawed vertebrates). Sower gives over 550 million years for the agnathan lineage. This dates the hormonal axis; the brain circuits of desire (preoptic area, ventromedial hypothalamus) are not dated by a source read here. The field value ~500Myr sexual is about right for the axis. Group T: crown vertebrates at least 457.5 (fossil, soft max 636.1), molecular 459.3 to 533.8; wording follows T's suggestion.

mechanism_ages.part: human pair bonding
mechanism_ages.age_label: about 2 to 4 million years (contested)
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the human form: the hominin pair bond, evolved in the human line after the split from chimpanzees; it is not inherited from early mammals, where social monogamy arose about 60 separate times
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest sources: Reno et al. 2003 (A. afarensis dimorphism like modern humans, placing the pair bond about 4 million years ago) against Gordon et al. 2008 (gorilla-like dimorphism, so later, with reduced dimorphism by early Homo about 2 million years ago); main weakness: mating systems are inferred from fossil body-size dimorphism, which Plavcan 2012 and Schacht and Kramer 2019 call unreliable.
mechanism_ages.note: The early side (about 4 million years, australopithecines) rests on Reno et al.; Lovejoy 2009 on Ardipithecus, named in the dispatch, was not read in full and is not used; the late side (early Homo, about 2 million years) on Gordon et al. and the reduced dimorphism in early Homo. Weight leans slightly to the later date: Schacht and Kramer report a general consensus that dimorphism was greater in the past and fell over time, and they cite several analyses that find A. afarensis strongly dimorphic (Lockwood et al. 1996 and 2007, Gordon et al. 2008); neither side is decisive. Fisher E193 (3.2 million years, Lucy) sits inside the range and is a trade-book theoretical claim. Hard outer bound: the human-chimpanzee split (group T: 6.5 to 10, fossil, contested).

mechanism_ages.part: C-tactile (CT) touch afferents
mechanism_ages.age_label: at least about 60 million years, probably under 90 (placental mammals)
mechanism_ages.dates_what: the basic nerve channel as shown so far: slow unmyelinated touch fibres in hairy skin recorded in humans, monkeys, cats and rodents, so present in their common placental ancestor
mechanism_ages.grade_line: Strongest source: single-fibre recordings by several groups in cats, monkeys and humans (reviewed by Liljencrantz and Olausson 2014), with a molecular rodent counterpart (Vrontou et al. 2013); main weakness: few placental species, no marsupial or monotreme data, and homology rests on similar response properties.
mechanism_ages.note: Clade: crown Boreoeutheria (common ancestor of primates, rodents and cats). The field value ~200Myr (mammalian) assumes all mammals have CTs; that is not shown. If CTs are found in marsupials or monotremes the age rises to crown Theria or crown Mammalia. Grooming and allogrooming are not dated by any source read here. Group T has no node for the primate-rodent-carnivore ancestor (Boreoeutheria). It contains crown primates, so it is older than 56 (T crown primates fossil minimum), and it is younger than crown placentals (T: 61.6 to 164.6 fossil, 87.9 to 90.4 molecular). The max is the crown placental soft maximum, not an estimate.

challenges_set_aside.title: Depression as sickness behavior? A test of the host defense hypothesis in a high pathogen population (Tsimane)
challenges_set_aside.reason: Refiled as support. The scores show low mood firing on its own triggers, here immune activation, in a forager-horticulturalist population, which is what OF2 predicts. One population with no matched comparison cannot score falsifier 1.

challenges_set_aside.title: Functional disability and social conflict increase risk of depression in older adulthood among Bolivian forager-farmers (Tsimane), prevalence finding
challenges_set_aside.reason: Set aside as a weak test and moved out of the core set. It is one cross-sectional sample, and its comparison with industrial prevalence runs across questionnaires that are not equivalent. The study's correlates (disability, a lost provider role, conflict) stay in the atlas.
